claim.qualifier: Ford's published peak DC fast-charge acceptance rate for Extended Range trim. The number is accurate; the framing as 'fast charging' is the editorial concern.
claim.verbatim_quote: The maximum DC fast charging acceptance rate is 150 kilowatts, very slow considering the 131-kilowatt-hour battery pack.

sources.name: Consumer Reports — Ford F-150 Lightning overview

reality.qualifier: 150 kW peak ÷ 131 kWh pack = 1.15C. Modern long-range EV trucks (Rivian R1T 220 kW peak / 135 kWh = 1.63C, Cybertruck advertised similar) deliver 1.5–2.0C peaks. Practically: ~45–55 minutes for 10–80% on the Lightning vs. 18–25 minutes for higher-C-rate competitors.
reality.verbatim_quote: very slow considering the 131 kilowatt-hour battery pack

narrative_one_liner: Lightning's 150 kW peak is real but unusually low (1.15C) for a 131 kWh battery; competitors do 1.5–2.0C.
narrative: Ford advertises 150 kW peak DC fast-charging on the Extended Range Lightning. While the number is accurate, it is unusually low relative to the 131 kWh battery pack — roughly half the C-rate of competitors like the Rivian R1T (220 kW on a similarly-sized pack). Consumer Reports flagged this as 'very slow considering the 131 kilowatt-hour battery pack.' Real-world impact: a 10–80% road-trip charge takes 45+ minutes vs. 20-ish for the Rivian.
methodology_notes: Single Tier-2 source provides the editorial framing (CR). The 150 kW number is Ford's own (Tier 4). The C-rate framing is our own derivation from publicly available battery sizes; we treat it as analytical commentary rather than an independent measurement.
caveats: kind=categorical because this is not a measurement gap — Ford's 150 kW number is correct. The deception is the framing of '150 kW' as 'fast charging' when comparable platforms deliver substantially higher C-rates.
C-rate calculation uses total pack kWh; usable kWh would yield a slightly different C-rate but doesn't change the conclusion.
Single-Tier-2 source; downgraded to grade B.
alternative_explanations: Lower C-rate may be deliberate engineering choice for battery longevity; this is a defensible trade-off but is not communicated to buyers.
Ford may have selected slower charging acceptance for thermal-management simplicity; again, a defensible choice that is not disclosed.
